title: Android installation
headings: Step 3: Start it and get a shell
text: Android installation # Everything on Android happens in the app, from installing the backend to opening a shell in a running container. This page takes you from a rooted phone to that shell. Before you start # You need two things. Root. KernelSU is the recommended root method. Magisk and APatch work as well. Their root shells carry a seccomp filter that blocks what a container runtime needs, which is why the backend runs as a daemon started at boot rather than from the shell. That is the default, and the reboot the app asks for after installing is all it takes. A kernel with container support. Most stock kernels are missing options that Droidspaces needs, especially PID and IPC namespaces. The kernel configuration guide lists them and explains how to build a kernel with them. If you would rather not build one, the community-supported devices page links to kernels other users have built. The app tells you on first launch whether your kernel is supported. Caution GrapheneOS is not supported. It blocks system calls that container isolation depends on, root or not. SuSFS is not supported. If you use it anyway, turn off "Hide sus mounts for all processes" in its settings or containers will not boot, and do not report bugs seen with it enabled. Step 1: Install the app # Download the APK from the latest release and install it. On KernelSU and APatch, allow root for the Droidspaces app in your root manager first. Magisk asks when the app requests it. Open the app and tap Get Started . Tap Check Root Access and, on Magisk, allow the request. The app installs the backend on its own: the droidspaces binary and a static BusyBox go to /data/local/Droidspaces/bin , and a small boot module goes to your root manager so the daemon and your containers can start at boot. This takes a few seconds. Read the result. "Droidspaces backend installed successfully" means your kernel passed the probe. If it says the kernel has no Droidspaces support, go to the kernel configuration guide before continuing. Reboot when the app asks. The reboot applies the SELinux rules the backend needs and starts the daemon. After the reboot, on a supported kernel, the Home tab shows "Backend: Installed" with a "DAEMON" chip, and your kernel version, SELinux status and architecture underneath. Step 2: Install a container # Open the Containers tab and tap + . You get two choices. From the repository # Repository opens a list of distributions built for Droidspaces, filtered to your device's architecture. Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Arch, Alpine, OpenWrt and others are there, and some come with a desktop environment already wired up. Pick a distribution and tap Download . The file goes to your Downloads folder, and a notification tells you when it is done. Tap Install on the same card. For more distributions, tap Manage Repositories in the same sheet and subscribe to the Linux Containers mirror: content_copy https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Droidspaces/linuxcontainers-mirror/refs/heads/main/rootfs.json Those images are stock upstream builds. The installer applies the same Android fixes to them, but they come without the extras of the official builds, such as a preconfigured desktop. From a file # Install from file takes a rootfs archive you already have on the phone. It must be a .tar.xz or .tar.gz . A container exported from another phone with Export container as tarball works here too, and its settings are filled in for you. The setup wizard # Both paths end in the same wizard. Container Setup : give the container a name. The hostname defaults to the name. Container configuration : the defaults are right for a first container. NAT networking gives it internet with no setup. Every toggle on this page is explained in container settings , and you can change any of them later from the container's menu. Storage : leave Use Sparse Image on. The rootfs then lives in a single ext4 image file, which is more reliable on Android's storage than a directory. The size you pick is the maximum; the file only grows as the container uses space. Choose a folder puts the image on an SD card or USB drive instead of internal storage. Installation Summary : check it and tap install. The app validates the archive, extracts it and applies a set of fixes that every container needs on Android, such as the network groups Android requires for socket access and a journald configuration that does not fill the phone with kernel logs. Installing takes one to a few minutes depending on the distribution. Step 3: Start it and get a shell # On the Containers tab, tap Start on the new container. A log window opens and shows the boot as it happens. Close it once the boot is done, and the card shows "RUNNING" and the container's PID. Open the Panel tab. Running containers appear here with their uptime, IP address, CPU and RAM. Tap Terminal on the card, pick a user, and you are in. The terminal keeps running in the background when you leave the screen, so you can come back to the same session later. If you prefer Termux or another terminal app, tap the container's card on the Panel tab to open its details, pick a user under Available Users and tap Copy login . Paste the command into a root shell. Checking requirements later # Settings has a Requirements page. Check Requirements runs every probe the backend has and tells you which kernel options are missing, which is the first thing to look at when a feature is greyed out in a container's settings. Next: Linux installation On Android you can skip ahead. Read these next: Android app guide , Container settings and Display, audio and desktop .

title: Linux installation
text: Linux installation # Droidspaces is one static binary on Linux. Any current distribution has everything it needs, and the only requirement is root. Step 1: Install the binary # Every release ships .deb packages for amd64, arm64, armhf, i386 and riscv64, and a tarball with the binary for each architecture. On Debian, Ubuntu and their derivatives: bash content_copy sudo dpkg -i droidspaces_*_amd64.deb On anything else, extract the tarball and copy the binary for your CPU somewhere on your PATH . uname -m tells you which one: x86_64 , aarch64 , armv7l (use armhf ), i686 (use x86 ) or riscv64 . bash content_copy tar -xzf droidspaces-v*.tar.gz sudo install -m 755 droidspaces-v*/x86_64/droidspaces /usr/local/bin/droidspaces Step 2: Check the system # bash content_copy sudo droidspaces check Every line should pass. The optional ones at the bottom cover features such as bridges, macvlan, IPv6 NAT and resource limits, and a missing one only disables that feature. Step 3: Get a rootfs # A container needs a root filesystem of the distribution you want to run. The Linux Containers image server has clean builds of most distributions. Browse to one, for example ubuntu/noble/amd64/default/ , and download rootfs.tar.xz . Important Extract with sudo . Without it the files inside the container are not owned by root, setuid bits are lost, and sudo and several services inside the container stop working. You can keep the rootfs in a directory or in an ext4 image file. The image is one file you can copy to another machine or phone, and it keeps the container's filesystem separate from the host's. Use whichever you prefer. A directory: bash content_copy mkdir ubuntu sudo tar -xf rootfs.tar.xz -C ubuntu An ext4 image (the file is sparse, so a 16 GB image takes only the space the container uses): bash content_copy truncate -s 16G ubuntu.img mkfs.ext4 -L ubuntu ubuntu.img mkdir mnt sudo mount ubuntu.img mnt sudo tar -xf rootfs.tar.xz -C mnt sudo umount mnt rmdir mnt Step 4: Start, enter, stop # bash content_copy sudo droidspaces --name = ubuntu --rootfs = /path/to/ubuntu start # or, for an image: sudo droidspaces --name = ubuntu --rootfs-img = /path/to/ubuntu.img start sudo droidspaces --name = ubuntu enter sudo droidspaces --name = ubuntu stop The flags you pass to the first start are saved in the container's config file, so later starts only need --name . droidspaces show lists what is running. Optional: run the daemon # The CLI works without a daemon on Linux. Running one lets members of a droidspaces group use the CLI without sudo , and restarts cleanly with the system. The repository has a systemd unit: bash content_copy sudo groupadd droidspaces sudo usermod -aG droidspaces " $USER " sudo cp init/systemd-service/droidspaces.service /etc/systemd/system/ sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl enable --now droidspaces The unit expects the binary at /usr/bin/droidspaces , which is where the .deb puts it. Edit ExecStart if yours is elsewhere. Log out and in again for the group to apply. Previous: Android installation | Next: Android app guide

title: Android app guide
text: Android app guide # The app has three tabs along the bottom, Home , Containers and Panel , and a gear icon in the top right for Settings . This page goes through them in that order. If you have not installed a container yet, start with the installation guide . Home # A status card says whether the backend is installed and up to date, which version it is, and whether the daemon is running. Below it are the number of installed and running containers and the device's kernel version, SELinux state, Android version and architecture. The card at the bottom opens the installation guide. "Backend: Update available" appears after an app update. Tap it to install the new backend; running containers are not affected. Containers # Every installed container has a card with its name, state, hostname, network mode, image size and resource limits, plus the options that are turned on. Start boots the container. A log window opens and shows the backend's output live, and you can close it once the operation finishes; Stop and Restart do the same. Once the container is running the card shows its PID and the buttons change to Stop and Restart . Press and hold a card for its menu: Edit Container Configuration : the same form as at install time. Every setting on it is explained in container settings . Changes apply at the next start. Migrate to a sparse image : converts a directory container to an ext4 image file. Resize the sparse image : changes the ceiling of an image container. Export container as tarball : packs the rootfs and its settings into a .tar.gz you can install on another phone. Environment variables are left out unless you choose to include them, since they often hold secrets. Uninstall Container : stops the container if it is running and deletes its rootfs and settings. You type the name to confirm. See uninstallation for what stays behind. The + button adds a container, from the Repository or Install from file . Repository # A list of distributions built for Droidspaces, filtered to your device's architecture. Search by name. Download fetches the tarball into your Downloads folder and shows progress on the card; a notification tells you when it is done, and the button turns into Install . A download that fails gets a Retry button, and a tarball downloaded earlier is recognised the next time you open the sheet. Manage Repositories in the sheet's header lets you subscribe to other feeds that publish a rootfs.json . The Linux Containers mirror is the one worth adding, for distributions and versions the official repository does not build: content_copy https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Droidspaces/linuxcontainers-mirror/refs/heads/main/rootfs.json Install from file # Picks a .tar.xz or .tar.gz rootfs archive from the phone's storage. A container exported from Droidspaces carries its settings and they are filled into the wizard, with a warning page first so you can review them. Any other rootfs tarball works too, as long as it has an init system. The setup wizard # Name and hostname, then the configuration form, then storage, then a summary. The installation guide walks through it, and container settings explains every toggle. Panel # Only running containers appear here, each with its uptime, IP address, CPU and RAM. With a memory or CPU limit set, usage is shown against the limit. Terminal opens a shell straight from the card, and a container with Anland Display on gets a Launch Anland button next to it once its desktop is up. Tapping anywhere else on the card opens the container's details. Container details # Container Info : distribution, hostname, uptime, IP address, CPU and RAM. Terminal : tap Open for a shell. When sessions are already running, the card says so and tapping it brings them back. Available Users : the user accounts in the rootfs. Pick one and tap Copy login to get a droidspaces enter command for that user on the clipboard, for use in Termux or any other root shell. Disk Usage : space used and total. Init System : tap Manage to control services. What you get depends on the init system. Managing services # Systemd. The list shows every unit with its state and is filterable: all, enabled, disabled, masked, static, or units in an abnormal state. Each one can be started, stopped, restarted, enabled, disabled or masked, and View logs shows its journal. Inspect unit opens the unit's properties, dependencies and systemctl status output, and Edit override writes a drop-in for it, so you can change a service's settings from the phone without a text editor in the container. OpenRC and OpenWrt (procd) get the same list with start, stop, restart, enable and disable, and reload on OpenWrt. Terminal # The built-in terminal opens a shell in the container as the user you pick. Tabs are labelled user@hostname ; the + tab opens another session, and asks for the user each time. Sessions run in a foreground service, so they survive leaving the screen, switching apps and the screen turning off, and the notification has an exit button and a wake lock toggle. Pinch to zoom changes the text size. Tapping the terminal opens the keyboard. The Terminal page under Settings has the font, with a custom monospace font import, the starting text size, a dark mode for the terminal page only, a confirmation before a tab closes, and Open Keyboard On Tap . Turn that one off when you work in an editor, so a tap only moves the cursor; a keyboard button then appears in the terminal to open and close the keyboard. Settings # Backend Reinstall Backend : writes the binaries and the boot module again. Use it if the Home tab reports the backend as corrupted. Daemon Mode : on by default. The backend runs as a system daemon started at boot, outside the root shell, which gets past the seccomp filter Magisk and APatch put on root shells. Leave it on; changing it needs a reboot. Integrate Droidspaces to the system path : puts droidspaces on the PATH of every root shell through the boot module, so you can type droidspaces instead of /data/local/Droidspaces/bin/droidspaces . Read the warning on the toggle: on OverlayFS-based module systems it causes a boot loop. Auto Boot Priority : the order in which containers with Run at Boot start. Drag to reorder. A gateway container goes above the containers that route through it. Requirements : lists the kernel options Droidspaces needs, with a copy button for kernel builders, and Check Requirements runs every probe against the running kernel. Appearance : language, light and dark theme, AMOLED black, the system colour palette on Android 12 and newer, accent colour, and the terminal settings above. Updates : check for a new app release. Debugging : Generate a bug report collects logs and device information into one file to attach to an issue. Experimental : Use the 64-bit backend appears only when the ROM is 32-bit on a 64-bit kernel, and switches the backend to the 64-bit build. About : version, developers, links to the source, the Telegram channel and the contributors. Where the data is # Everything the backend creates is under /data/local/Droidspaces : the binaries in bin/ , each container's rootfs or image and its container.config in Containers/<name>/ , and logs in Logs/ . The app only reads and writes there; uninstalling the app does not touch it, and the daemon keeps running. Previous: Linux installation | Next: Container settings

title: Container settings
headings: Termux:X11 Extra Flags and VirGL Extra Flags
text: Container settings # Each setting below is one toggle in the app's container configuration, and one flag on the command line. They are listed in the order the app shows them. The CLI flag and the key it writes to the container's config file are given with each one, so this page serves both the app and the CLI. How settings are stored # Every container has a container.config file of key=value lines. The app writes it from the configuration form. On the CLI, the flags you pass to the first start are saved into it, so later starts only need --name . Flags passed to a later start or restart update the file; --reset returns it to defaults while keeping the name and rootfs. A change takes effect the next time the container starts. In the app, the container's menu has Edit Container Configuration . Networking # Network Mode # --net=MODE , key net_mode . The default is nat . Mode What the container gets Use it when NAT Its own network stack and a private address, with internet through the host. Nothing to set up. The host's active connection is followed as it changes between Wi-Fi, mobile data and Ethernet. You want a container that just has internet. This is the right choice for almost everything. Gateway Its own network stack, on a LAN owned by another running container, usually OpenWrt, which does DHCP, DNS, firewalling, routing and VPN for it. You want a VPN kill switch, DNS filtering, or several containers on one isolated LAN behind one router. Macvlan Its own MAC address on a wired network the phone is plugged into, and an address from that network's router. No NAT. The container should be a first-class device on your home LAN, reachable without port forwarding. Needs a USB Ethernet adapter on a phone. Host The host's own network stack, shared. A program needs an interface only the host has. Services bind host ports directly, and a network manager inside the container can break the phone's connectivity. None A network stack with only loopback. The container must be offline. Networking from zero explains all five in depth, including how to set up an OpenWrt gateway. Static IP Address # --nat-ip=IP , key static_nat_ip . NAT mode only. Fixes the container's address in the 172.28.0.0/16 range. Without it the address is derived from the container's PID and can change between starts, which matters when another device or a port forward on your router has it written down. Upstream Interface # --upstream=IFACE[,IFACE...] , key upstream_interfaces . NAT mode only. Leave it empty and the container follows whatever connection the host is using. Set it and the container's internet goes out through the listed interfaces only, first one that is up and has internet wins. Wildcards work, and rmnet* is the way to name mobile data, whose interface number changes between reconnects. tun0 : the container can only reach the internet through a VPN app running on the phone. When the VPN is down, the container is offline. rmnet* : the container stays on mobile data while the phone uses Wi-Fi. Turn on "Mobile data always active" in Developer Options for this. wlan0,rmnet* : Wi-Fi when available, mobile data otherwise. Port Forwarding # --port=[HOST:]CONTAINER[/tcp|udp] , key port_forwards . NAT mode only. Makes a service inside the container reachable on a port of the host, from the host itself and from any network it is on. --port=22 maps the same port on both sides, --port=8080:80 maps host 8080 to container 80, and --port=1000-2000:1000-2000 maps a range of the same size. Without a protocol, both TCP and UDP are forwarded. Repeat the flag or separate entries with commas. Disable IPv6 # --disable-ipv6 , key disable_ipv6 . Turns IPv6 off inside the container. In NAT mode the container normally gets IPv6 as well as IPv4, provided the kernel has IPv6 NAT; without it the app holds this toggle on. In host mode the setting reaches the host's own stack, which can break VPN apps on the phone. DNS Servers # --dns=SERVER[,SERVER...] , key dns_servers . Without it, NAT, host and none mode containers use Cloudflare and Google's public resolvers. Gateway and macvlan containers use whatever DNS their LAN's DHCP server hands out, which is what you want when the gateway filters ads or resolves local names, so set this only to override that on purpose. Integration and hardware # Android Storage # --enable-android-storage , key enable_android_storage . Android only. Mounts the phone's shared storage at /storage/emulated/0 inside the container, so your photos, downloads and documents are reachable from Linux. Hardware Access # --hw-access , key enable_hw_access . Gives the container the host's real /dev : GPU, USB devices, sensors, input devices, and every block device, partitions and SD card included. The container behaves like a Linux machine with that hardware. Turn it on for USB peripherals, for a desktop with GPU acceleration on Linux, or for anything that needs a device node the GPU toggle does not cover. Caution Raw block devices are in there. A wrong dd or mkfs inside the container destroys the phone's partitions. Use this only with a container you trust, and do not report bugs seen with it on. The app makes you type a confirmation for that reason. The six host virtual terminals, tty1 to tty6 , stay hidden even with hardware access on, because a systemd container would otherwise put its login prompt on the host console. --allow-vts reveals them. The app has no toggle for it. GPU Access # --gpu , key enable_gpu_mode . The middle ground. The container keeps its private /dev and only the GPU render nodes are mirrored into it, so programs can use the GPU and nothing else on the host is exposed. Mirrored nodes are owned by a droidspaces-gpu group that root belongs to; add other users to that group with usermod . Hardware Access turns this on as well. Known GPU families: Mesa DRI render nodes on Intel, AMD and most ARM SoCs, Qualcomm Adreno ( kgsl ), ARM Mali, NVIDIA, PowerVR and the DMA heaps these drivers need. Configure Termux:X11 # --x11 , key enable_x11 . Android: starts the Termux:X11 server when the container starts, mounts its socket into the container, and sets DISPLAY for every login shell. Needs the Termux and Termux:X11 apps and the one-time setup in the display guide . Linux: mounts the host's X11 socket so GUI programs in the container open on your desktop. Anland Display # --anland , key enable_anland . Android only. Starts the Anland display daemon for the container, so a Wayland compositor patched for Anland can show its desktop in the Anland app. Needs GPU Access, a patched compositor in the container and the Anland app on the phone, and it replaces Termux:X11 rather than adding to it. The Anland guide walks through it. Configure VirGL 3D Acceleration # --virgl , key enable_virgl . Android only. Starts the VirGL server in Termux alongside Termux:X11 and sets GALLIUM_DRIVER=virpipe in the container, so OpenGL programs render on the phone's GPU instead of in software. The right choice on Mali and PowerVR GPUs. On Qualcomm, Turnip inside the container with GPU Access is faster; the display guide compares them. Configure PulseAudio # --pulse-audio , key enable_pulseaudio . Android only. Starts a PulseAudio server in Termux, mounts its socket into the container and sets PULSE_SERVER , so anything that plays sound in the container comes out of the phone's speaker. Resource limits # --memory=SIZE , --cpus=COUNT and --pids-limit=N , keys memory_limit , cpu_quota with cpu_period , and pids_limit . Off by default; a container shares everything the device has. Limit memory : --memory=512M or --memory=2G . The container cannot grow past it into the device's swap, so at the limit its own OOM killer ends a process inside it instead of the phone slowing down as zram fills. Everything inside the container, free and fastfetch included, reports usage against this limit and no swap. Allow swap : --allow-swap , key allow_swap . Lets a memory-limited container use the device's swap past its limit, as it could before the cap, and shows it the device's swap. droidspaces info and show --json say whether a running container may swap. Limit CPU : --cpus=1.5 gives the container one and a half cores' worth of time, spread over all cores. Limit processes : the most processes and threads the container may have at once, minimum 16. A systemd distribution needs a few hundred. Each limit needs its cgroup controller in the kernel: CONFIG_MEMCG , CONFIG_CFS_BANDWIDTH and CONFIG_CGROUP_PIDS . The app greys out a limit the kernel cannot enforce and names the missing option; the CLI skips it at start with a warning. Stock Android kernels often lack the CPU and process ones. droidspaces info prints the limits in force and current usage. One gap: a program that asks the kernel directly through sysinfo() rather than reading /proc still sees the host's memory and load. OpenWrt's LuCI does this. The limit is enforced all the same. Security and boot # SELinux Permissive # --selinux-permissive , key selinux_permissive . Android and supported Linux distros only. Switches the host's SELinux to permissive while the container runs, and back to enforcing when the last container that asked for it stops. Allow Sandboxing # --allow-sandboxing , key allow_sandboxing . Off by default. Turn it on when something inside the container builds its own sandbox: rootless Docker or Podman, Flatpak, bwrap, Firefox, Chromium. They all create a user namespace and mount their own /proc inside it, and a stock container blocks both. With the toggle on, user namespaces are allowed and the container gets the pristine /proc and read-only /sys instances the kernel requires for that, under /run/droidspaces/ . The cost is that root in the container can reach the host's live sysctl tree through that pristine /proc , so this is a statement of trust in the container's root user. Needs CONFIG_USER_NS , reported by droidspaces check as user namespace support. For Docker inside the container, put {"userns-remap": "default"} in /etc/docker/daemon.json and restart it. Volatile Mode # --volatile , key volatile_mode . Every write goes to RAM and is thrown away when the container stops; the rootfs is never changed. Good for trying a package, for a clean environment on every boot, or for breaking things on purpose. Needs OverlayFS in the kernel. On Android it needs a sparse image rootfs, because OverlayFS on most Android kernels refuses an f2fs directory as its base. Force Cgroup V1 # --force-cgroupv1 , key force_cgroupv1 . Makes the container use the legacy cgroup v1 hierarchy even when the host offers v2. For old Android kernels, 4.9 and earlier, whose cgroup v2 is missing the controllers systemd expects, which makes systemd misread the environment and fail to boot. Leave it off unless a systemd container will not boot on such a kernel. Privileged Mode # --privileged=TAG[,TAG...] , key privileged . Removes security barriers one at a time: nomask : /proc and /sys are not masked. /sys stays read-only unless Hardware Access is on. nocaps : no capabilities are dropped; root in the container is full root. noseccomp : no system call filtering. shared : mounts made in the container propagate to the host. full : all of the above. Each one is a hole in the container's isolation. Nothing in ordinary use needs them; Allow Sandboxing covers Flatpak, bwrap and rootless Docker on its own. Bugs seen with privileged mode on are not accepted, and the app asks you to confirm that. Run at Boot # Key run_at_boot , with run_at_boot_priority . App only. Starts the container when the phone boots, before the lock screen, through the boot module the app installed. Containers start in the order set under Settings , Auto Boot Priority ; put a gateway container before the containers that route through it. Advanced options # Environment Variables # --env=PATH , key env_file . A file of KEY=value lines, one per line, # for comments. The variables are set for the container's init and for every enter and run session. The app edits the file for you. Bind Mounts # --bind=SRC:DEST[:ro] , key bind_mounts . Makes a host directory visible inside the container at DEST , read-only with :ro . Repeat the flag or separate entries with commas. The destination must be an absolute path inside the container and cannot be / . A source that is missing at start is skipped with a warning rather than failing the boot. Custom Init Binary # --init=PATH , key custom_init . The program to run as PID 1 instead of /sbin/init . For a distribution that keeps its init elsewhere, or to start a shell as PID 1 when debugging a rootfs that will not boot. Termux:X11 Extra Flags and VirGL Extra Flags # --tx11-flags="..." , key tx11_extra_flags , and --virgl-flags="..." , key virgl_extra_flags . Extra arguments for the Termux:X11 and VirGL servers Droidspaces starts. Shown in the app only when the matching toggle is on. Storage # Chosen once, when the container is installed. Sparse image : the rootfs lives in one ext4 image file that Droidspaces loop-mounts at start. The CLI equivalent is --rootfs-img=PATH , which also accepts a block device. The image behaves the same whatever filesystem the host uses, which matters on Android's f2fs, and it is one file to copy when you move the container. Images are checked with e2fsck when their superblock says they need it. The size you pick is a ceiling; the file grows as the container uses space. The app can Resize the sparse image later, and Migrate to a sparse image converts a directory container. Directory : the rootfs is a plain directory, --rootfs=PATH on the CLI. Simpler to look into from the host. On Android, use it only if the image path is not possible. Storage location : internal storage by default, or any folder you pick, including an SD card or USB drive. A location that cannot hold a directory rootfs forces the sparse image. Things with no toggle # Init systems. Any init that can run as PID 1 works: systemd, OpenRC, runit, s6, SysVinit, OpenWrt's procd. The container's /sbin/init must exist, or you name another with Custom Init Binary. The app's container details recognise systemd, OpenRC and procd and let you manage their services. Hostname. --hostname=NAME , key hostname . Defaults to the container name. Foreground mode. --foreground on the CLI attaches your terminal to the container's console for the whole boot, which is the best way to see why a container does not come up. title: Linux CLI
text: Command line reference # The droidspaces binary is the same on Linux and Android, and so are its commands and flags. On Android the app installs it at /data/local/Droidspaces/bin/droidspaces , and the Integrate Droidspaces to the system path setting puts it on the PATH of root shells. Flags and the command can come in any order, short and long forms are interchangeable, and = is optional: droidspaces -n web start and droidspaces start --name=web are the same. droidspaces docs shows the same reference in a pager, offline. Commands # Command What it does start Boots a container. The first start needs --name and --rootfs or --rootfs-img ; after that the saved config supplies them. stop Shuts the container down cleanly. --name=a,b,c stops several. restart Stops and starts again. Image mounts are kept, so it is fast. enter [user] Opens a shell inside a running container, as root by default. run [--] <cmd> Runs one command inside a running container and returns. --user picks the account, --stdin pipes your input in. Anything after run belongs to the command, and -- lets the command itself start with a dash. show Lists running containers. With --json , JSON with distribution, hostname, IP, uptime, CPU and RAM for each. info Shows a container's settings and state. With --json , JSON. pid Prints the PID of the container's init, or NONE . scan Finds running containers whose host-side records were lost and registers them again. check Probes the kernel for everything Droidspaces uses. With --json , JSON with one 0 or 1 per probe and requirements_met . daemon Starts the daemon. --foreground keeps it attached to the terminal, for a service manager. mode Prints daemon if a daemon is answering, otherwise direct . docs , help , version The built-in documentation, the flag summary, and the version. Every command except check , docs , help , version and mode needs root. When exactly one container is running, --name can be left out of stop , restart , enter , run , info and pid . If a daemon is running, the CLI hands the command to it, so members of the droidspaces group can use the CLI without sudo . DS_NO_PROXY=1 in the environment makes the binary do the work itself. Flags # Each flag that configures the container is saved in its config file on start , so it only has to be given once. Container settings explains what each one does and when to use it; this table is the syntax. Rootfs and identity Flag Value Config key -r , --rootfs directory with the rootfs rootfs_path -i , --rootfs-img ext4 image file or block device rootfs_path -n , --name container name; a Without it the command gets nothing. --json JSON output from show , info and check . The config file # A plain key=value file, one key per line, with the keys from the tables above. Droidspaces looks for it in this order: the file named by --config , then container.config next to the rootfs, then Containers/<name>/container.config in the workspace. The workspace is /var/lib/Droidspaces on Linux and /data/local/Droidspaces on Android. ini content_copy name = web hostname = web rootfs_path = /var/lib/Droidspaces/Containers/web/rootfs.img net_mode = nat port_forwards = 80:80,443:443 bind_mounts = /srv/www:/var/www:ro memory_limit = 1073741824 cpu_quota = 200000 cpu_period = 100000 allow_sandboxing = 1 Boolean keys take 0 or 1 . title: Display, audio and desktop
headings: Three ways to render on Android
A desktop that starts at boot
text: Display, audio and desktop # On Android, Droidspaces starts the Termux:X11 display server, the VirGL server and the PulseAudio server for you when the matching toggles are on, and sets DISPLAY , GALLIUM_DRIVER and PULSE_SERVER inside the container. Turn on the toggles, start the container, and graphical programs open in the Termux:X11 app with sound from the phone's speaker. This page covers the one-time setup, the three ways to render, sound, a desktop that starts at boot, and the Linux side. For a Wayland desktop such as KDE Plasma there is a second path, covered on the Anland page. Important Droidspaces does not ship Termux:X11, VirGL or PulseAudio. They are Termux packages. Droidspaces starts and stops them and bridges their sockets into the container. One-time setup on Android # Install the Termux and Termux:X11 apps. Get both from the same source, F-Droid or GitHub, so they are signed by the same key. In Termux, run the setup script. It installs Termux:X11, VirGL and PulseAudio into Termux and patches PulseAudio's configuration for Android's audio stack: bash content_copy curl -fsSL https://github.com/ravindu644/Droidspaces-OSS/raw/refs/heads/dev/scripts/setup-termux.sh | bash That is all. You do not start anything in Termux yourself afterwards. Tip The official XFCE images in the repository start XFCE on their own. Install one, turn on Configure Termux:X11 , start the container and open the Termux:X11 app. The desktop is there. The auto-boot section explains how it is wired, in case you want the same for another desktop. The display variables are set for login shells through /etc/profile.d . In zsh , fish or another shell that skips it, run source /run/droidspaces.env once after the container boots. Three ways to render on Android # Works on Speed Toggles llvmpipe every device software rendering, fine for a desktop and 2D apps Configure Termux:X11 VirGL Mali, PowerVR and other non-Qualcomm GPUs hardware accelerated through a bridge in Termux Configure Termux:X11 and Configure VirGL 3D Acceleration Turnip Qualcomm Adreno near native, the GPU is driven from inside the container GPU Access and Configure Termux:X11, VirGL off llvmpipe # Turn on Configure Termux:X11 in the container's configuration and start the container. When the Termux:X11 app shows its X-shaped cursor, the server is ready. Inside the container, glxgears or startxfce4 opens in Termux:X11. Nothing else to set up, and no hardware access needed. VirGL # Turn on Configure Termux:X11 and Configure VirGL 3D Acceleration , then start the container. OpenGL calls in the container are sent to the VirGL server in Termux, which runs them on the phone's GPU. glxinfo | grep renderer inside the container names VirGL when it is working. If VirGL fails to start, put --angle-vulkan in the VirGL Extra Flags field to switch it to the Vulkan backend. Turnip # Turnip is Mesa's open source Vulkan driver for Adreno, and with Zink on top it gives OpenGL as well. The container talks to the GPU directly, so it needs the GPU nodes and a Mesa build with Turnip. Install Mesa with Turnip inside the container, following Mesa for Android Container . In the container's configuration, turn on GPU Access and Configure Termux:X11 , and make sure Configure VirGL 3D Acceleration is off. Add two environment variables under Advanced Options : content_copy MESA_LOADER_DRIVER_OVERRIDE=kgsl TU_DEBUG=noconform Start the container. Graphical programs now render on the GPU. A user other than root needs to be in the droidspaces-gpu group to open the GPU nodes: usermod -aG droidspaces-gpu <user> inside the container. Sound on Android # Turn on Configure PulseAudio and start the container. Droidspaces starts a PulseAudio server in Termux, where Android's audio system allows it to play, routes it to the speaker, mounts its socket into the container at /tmp/.pulse-socket and sets PULSE_SERVER . Anything that uses PulseAudio or PipeWire's PulseAudio compatibility plays through the phone. paplay file.wav is a quick test, and pactl info shows the connection. Whether sound works at all depends on the phone: the Android version, the vendor's audio HAL and the Termux PulseAudio build. On Samsung One UI 6.1 and newer, Droidspaces preloads a library the audio module needs; nothing to do on your side. A desktop that starts at boot # Droidspaces makes sure the X server's socket, /tmp/.X11-unix/X5 , exists before the container's init reaches graphical.target , so a systemd unit can start a desktop without racing it. The official XFCE images ship such a unit; the same pattern works for any desktop. The unit, /etc/systemd/system/xfce-autostart.service : ini content_copy [Unit] Description = XFCE Autostart After = graphical.target [Service] Type = simple User = root ExecCondition = /bin/sh -c "grep -q 'enable_x11=1' /run/droidspaces/container.config" ExecCondition = /bin/sh -c "test -S /tmp/.X11-unix/X5" ExecStart = /usr/local/bin/xfce-start Restart = on-failure [Install] WantedBy = graphical.target The two conditions keep the unit quiet when Termux:X11 is off or the socket is missing: systemd skips it instead of failing. The launcher, /usr/local/bin/xfce-start , loads the environment Droidspaces wrote and starts the desktop, as root or as the user named in XFCE_USER : sh content_copy #!/bin/sh ENV_FILE = /run/droidspaces.env CONFIG = /run/droidspaces/container.config if [ -f " $ENV_FILE " ] ; then . " $ENV_FILE " WHITELIST = $( sed -n 's/^export \([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*\)=.*/\1/p' " $ENV_FILE " | tr '\n' ',' | sed 's/,$//' ) else export DISPLAY = :5 WHITELIST = DISPLAY if grep -q 'enable_pulseaudio=1' " $CONFIG " 2 >/dev/null ; then export PULSE_SERVER = unix:/tmp/.pulse-socket WHITELIST = " $WHITELIST ,PULSE_SERVER" fi if grep -q 'enable_virgl=1' " $CONFIG " 2 >/dev/null ; then export GALLIUM_DRIVER = virpipe WHITELIST = " $WHITELIST ,GALLIUM_DRIVER" fi fi if [ -n " $XFCE_USER " ] ; then exec su -l -w " $WHITELIST " " $XFCE_USER " -c 'exec /usr/bin/startxfce4' else exec /usr/bin/startxfce4 fi To run the desktop as a normal user, create one in the container with useradd -m <user> and set XFCE_USER=<user> under Environment Variables in the container's configuration. su -l -w passes only the display and audio variables into that user's session. For another desktop, copy both files under new names, replace startxfce4 in the launcher with the desktop's start command, such as startplasma-x11 , and enable the unit with systemctl enable . The variable name XFCE_USER is only a convention; call it what you like. Linux # On a Linux host, GPU acceleration needs no bridge: the container uses the host's GPU through Mesa like any other program. Turn on Hardware Access , or GPU Access for the render nodes alone, with --hw-access or --gpu on the CLI. Allow the container to reach your X server: xhost +local: on the host. Start the container with --x11 , which mounts the host's X socket, and set DISPLAY=:0 , or whatever the host uses, in the container's environment file. Graphical programs started in the container then open on your desktop with hardware acceleration. Sound goes through the host's own PulseAudio or PipeWire socket if you bind-mount it; Droidspaces does not manage audio on Linux. Previous: Linux CLI | Next: Anland

title: Anland (Wayland)
text: Anland (Wayland) # Anland is an optional Wayland display path for Droidspaces. A Linux compositor patched for Anland, such as KWin or Weston, renders the desktop into GPU buffers. The Anland app displays those buffers on Android, while a small Droidspaces broker connects the container and the app over a Unix domain socket. Unlike Termux:X11, Anland is designed for Wayland compositors such as KDE Plasma Wayland. Anland handles the display path; Droidspaces still manages the container, rootfs, permissions, GPU access and startup. Qualcomm Snapdragon devices with Adreno GPUs are recommended. Anland relies on device-side GPU buffer sharing, and Qualcomm devices tend to be more compatible. More Anland guides # Anland user guide : Install Anland and connect to an Anland-capable Wayland desktop through chroot or Droidspaces. Anland settings guide : Configure input, display, connection, audio and window behavior in the Android app. Quick navigation # Requirements Step 1: Install an Anland backend Build it in the container Build a rootfs automatically Step 2: Install the Anland app Step 3: Configure the container Requirements # Before setting up Anland, make sure you have: An Android device supported by Droidspaces. Anland works with Droidspaces when Anland Display is enabled in the container configuration. A compositor backend patched for Anland. KWin is the main supported backend. See the Anland producers directory for available builds. A compatible GPU. Qualcomm Snapdragon devices with Adreno GPUs are recommended for better compatibility. Step 1: Install an Anland backend # The desktop in the container must use a compositor backend patched for Anland. An unpatched Wayland compositor cannot send its display to the Anland app. Build it in the container # Build the backend yourself if you want to choose a distribution or desktop environment, or need to debug the setup. Open a shell in the Droidspaces container. Clone the Anland source: bash content_copy git clone -b legacy https://github.com/SuperTurtleDev/anland.git Under producers , choose the directory for your desktop and distribution. KDE backend directories include: text content_copy producers/kde/ ├── anland_backend/ ├── Debian13_v5/ ├── Fedora43_v5/ └── ubuntu2604_v5/ As root, run build.sh in the matching directory. The script installs the required dependencies and Anland backend. Start the desktop with the project's startup.sh script. Build a rootfs automatically # For a ready-to-import rootfs, use Droidspaces-rootfs-Desktop-builder . Important The builder currently supports KDE Plasma, GNOME and niri desktops. Fork the project. Open its GitHub Actions page and find the 编译并发布Droidspaces Rootfs workflow. Run the workflow manually and select anland-wayland for the display backend. Wait for the build to finish. It usually takes about 15 minutes. Open the project's Releases page, download the generated rootfs package and import it into Droidspaces. If the KDE desktop is not configured to start automatically, enter the container as a regular user and run the command for your desktop: bash content_copy startplasma-wayland # KDE Plasma startplasmamobile # KDE Plasma Mobile gnome-session --session = gnome niri-anland Step 2: Install the Anland app # Download anland-v5.apk from the newest 5.x release on the Anland releases page . Droidspaces supports only Anland 5.x. The 6.x releases, marked "Latest" there, are a different app and do not work with it. Install the APK on your Android device. Grant it root access. With KernelSU or APatch, allow it in the manager app. With Magisk, open Anland once and accept the root prompt. Step 3: Configure the container # Edit the target container's configuration in Droidspaces. Required settings # Turn on GPU Access . Hardware Access also satisfies this requirement, but GPU Access is sufficient. Turn on Anland Display . Turn off Configure Termux:X11 . Anland and Termux:X11 use separate display paths with conflicting environment variables and services. Enabling Anland Display turns off Configure Termux:X11 for that container. On the CLI, enable Anland with --anland or the enable_anland config key. Important Use one display path per container. Keep the Termux:X11 configuration off while using Anland. Recommended settings # Configure PulseAudio: Leave this off because Anland has its own audio path. If PulseAudio was previously enabled, remove any existing PULSE_SERVER environment variable from the container so applications do not connect to the old server. SELinux Permissive: Leave this off and try Anland with SELinux enforcing first. If Anland cannot start or display anything on your device, you can temporarily enable this option to check for a compatibility issue. Allow Sandboxing: Enable this for KDE Plasma and similar desktop environments. It allows user namespaces, which can improve Plasma Wayland responsiveness. This weakens container isolation, so enable it only for containers you trust. Anland does not require privileged mode, noseccomp , nomask or other privileged options. Start the container, then tap its card on the Panel tab to open the container details. The Anland card below Terminal has a Launch button that opens the desktop in the Anland app. The button becomes active when the container starts and Droidspaces records the broker socket. The desktop appears after the compositor inside the container starts. Previous: Display, audio and desktop | Next: Kernel configuration

title: Kernel configuration
headings: CPU and process limits on GKI
Which kernel version to aim for
text: Kernel configuration # Droidspaces needs kernel features that most stock Android kernels leave out: PID and IPC namespaces, a few networking pieces and devtmpfs. This page is the list of options and patches for building a kernel that has them. The oldest supported kernel is 3.10. If you have never built an Android kernel, start with the Android kernel tutorials , and check the community-supported devices page first: someone may have built a kernel for your phone already. The steps differ between non-GKI kernels, 4.19 and older, and GKI kernels, 5.4 and newer. Non-GKI kernels (3.18 to 4.19) # These kernels take the options as they are, with no ABI to protect. Four steps. Step 1: The required options # Add these to your device's defconfig, or keep them as a fragment and merge it at build time: makefile content_copy # Kernel configurations for full DroidSpaces support # Copyright (C) 2026 ravindu644 <droidcasts@protonmail.com> # IPC mechanisms CONFIG_SYSCTL = y CONFIG_SYSVIPC = y CONFIG_POSIX_MQUEUE = y # Core namespace support CONFIG_NAMESPACES = y CONFIG_PID_NS = y CONFIG_UTS_NS = y CONFIG_IPC_NS = y # Seccomp support CONFIG_SECCOMP = y CONFIG_SECCOMP_FILTER = y # Control groups support CONFIG_CGROUPS = y CONFIG_CGROUP_DEVICE = y CONFIG_CGROUP_SCHED = y CONFIG_FAIR_GROUP_SCHED = y CONFIG_CGROUP_FREEZER = y CONFIG_CGROUP_NET_PRIO = y # Resource limits: --memory, --cpus, --pids-limit, in that order, then the # accounting that reports CPU usage on kernels before 4.15. # Optional: a limit whose option is missing is skipped with a warning CONFIG_MEMCG = y # Keeps a memory-limited container out of swap. Before 6.1 only; before 5.8 # also boot with swapaccount=1 unless CONFIG_MEMCG_SWAP_ENABLED=y CONFIG_MEMCG_SWAP = y CONFIG_CFS_BANDWIDTH = y CONFIG_CGROUP_PIDS = y CONFIG_CGROUP_CPUACCT = y # Device filesystem support CONFIG_DEVTMPFS = y # Overlay filesystem support (required for volatile mode) CONFIG_OVERLAY_FS = y # Enable xattr, posix acl support on tmpfs # For NixOS support CONFIG_TMPFS_POSIX_ACL = y CONFIG_TMPFS_XATTR = y # Firmware loading support CONFIG_FW_LOADER = y CONFIG_FW_LOADER_USER_HELPER = y CONFIG_FW_LOADER_COMPRESS = y # Droidspaces Network Isolation Support - NAT/none modes CONFIG_NET_NS = y CONFIG_VETH = y CONFIG_BRIDGE = y CONFIG_NETFILTER = y CONFIG_BRIDGE_NETFILTER = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_ADVANCED = y CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK = y CONFIG_IP_NF_IPTABLES = y CONFIG_IP_NF_FILTER = y CONFIG_NF_NAT = y CONFIG_NF_TABLES = y CONFIG_IP_NF_TARGET_MASQUERADE = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_TARGET_MASQUERADE = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_TARGET_TCPMSS = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_MATCH_ADDRTYPE = y CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK_NETLINK = y CONFIG_NF_NAT_REDIRECT = y CONFIG_IP_ADVANCED_ROUTER = y CONFIG_IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES = y # legacy compat CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK_IPV4 = y CONFIG_NF_NAT_IPV4 = y CONFIG_IP_NF_NAT = y # IPv6 in NAT mode (NAT66). Optional: without these, NAT containers are IPv4 only CONFIG_IPV6 = y CONFIG_IPV6_MULTIPLE_TABLES = y CONFIG_IP6_NF_IPTABLES = y CONFIG_IP6_NF_FILTER = y CONFIG_IP6_NF_MANGLE = y CONFIG_IP6_NF_NAT = y CONFIG_IP6_NF_TARGET_MASQUERADE = y # legacy compat CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK_IPV6 = y CONFIG_NF_NAT_IPV6 = y # Macvlan mode (--net=macvlan): a container straight on a wired LAN. # Optional: without it, macvlan mode is unavailable CONFIG_MACVLAN = y # Disable this on older kernels to make internet work CONFIG_ANDROID_PARANOID_NETWORK = n # Fix for docker unsafe procfs error CONFIG_USER_NS = y Step 2: Firewall support, optional # Only needed to run UFW or Fail2Ban inside a container, as in the home server recipe : makefile content_copy # UFW & FAIL2BAN CORE CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_MATCH_COMMENT = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_MATCH_STATE = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_MATCH_CONNTRACK = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_MATCH_MULTIPORT = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_MATCH_HL = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_TARGET_REJECT = y CONFIG_IP_NF_TARGET_REJECT = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_TARGET_LOG = y CONFIG_IP_NF_TARGET_ULOG = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_MATCH_RECENT = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_MATCH_LIMIT = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_MATCH_HASHLIMIT = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_MATCH_OWNER = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_MATCH_PKTTYPE = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_MATCH_MARK = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_TARGET_MARK = y CONFIG_IP_SET = y CONFIG_IP_SET_HASH_IP = y CONFIG_IP_SET_HASH_NET = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_SET = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_NETLINK_QUEUE = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_NETLINK_LOG = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_TARGET_NFLOG = y Step 3: Patches # Apply every patch under assets/resources/kernel-patches/non-GKI : bash content_copy patch -p1 < /path/to/patchfile.patch Step 4: Build, flash, check # Build and flash as usual for your device, then open the Droidspaces app and run Settings , Requirements , Check Requirements . Everything under "must have" and "recommended" should pass. GKI kernels (5.4 and newer) # Google's Generic Kernel Image keeps a fixed kernel ABI so that vendor modules built against the stock kernel keep loading. Several options Droidspaces needs, CONFIG_SYSVIPC , CONFIG_IPC_NS and CONFIG_POSIX_MQUEUE , add fields to core structures and shift the ABI. Turned on as they are, the phone bootloops when the vendor's modules refuse to load. The patches below move those fields into padding the ABI already reserves, so the options can go on without changing any offset. Step 1: The kABI patches # Important These are not optional. Without the patch for your kernel version, enabling the IPC options bootloops the device. 5.4 to 6.6: apply the SYSVIPC patch from kernel-patches/GKI/below-kernel-6.12 . Start with 001.GKI-below-6.12-fix_sysvipc_kabi_6_7_8.patch ; if the device bootloops, try the alternatives in the same folder, which use different padding slots. 5.10 and older: also apply 002.5.10_or_lower_use_android_abi_padding_for_posix_mqueue.patch from the same folder. 6.12 and newer: apply the patch in kernel-patches/GKI/kernel-6.12 . bash content_copy patch -p1 < /path/to/patchfile.patch Step 2: Edit the GKI defconfig # Edit arch/arm64/configs/gki_defconfig in place rather than adding a fragment. For each option below, find it in the file: change # CONFIG_X is not set to CONFIG_X=y , leave it alone if it is already on, and add it at the end if it is absent. Warning These options are ABI-safe together with the Step 1 patches. Do not turn on anything beyond them. The two resource limit options at the end are commented out on purpose; see CPU and process limits on GKI before touching them. makefile content_copy # Kernel configurations for full DroidSpaces support for GKI # Copyright (C) 2026 ravindu644 <droidcasts@protonmail.com> # IPC CONFIG_SYSVIPC = y CONFIG_POSIX_MQUEUE = y # Namespaces CONFIG_IPC_NS = y CONFIG_PID_NS = y # HW Access Support CONFIG_DEVTMPFS = y # Networking (Enhanced NAT support) CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_MATCH_ADDRTYPE = y # --- Below configs are optional but recommended --- # Fix for docker unsafe procfs error CONFIG_USER_NS = y # IPv6 in NAT mode (NAT66) CONFIG_IP6_NF_NAT = y CONFIG_IP6_NF_TARGET_MASQUERADE = y # Macvlan mode (--net=macvlan). kABI-safe: on a 5.15 GKI tree it changed none # of the 8423 exported symbols, and the driver is self-contained CONFIG_MACVLAN = y # UFW support CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_TARGET_REJECT = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_TARGET_LOG = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_MATCH_RECENT = y # Fail2ban support CONFIG_IP_SET = y CONFIG_IP_SET_HASH_IP = y CONFIG_IP_SET_HASH_NET = y CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_SET = y # Enable xattr, posix acl support on tmpfs # For NixOS support CONFIG_TMPFS_POSIX_ACL = y CONFIG_TMPFS_XATTR = y # Resource limits: --cpus and --pids-limit. CONFIG_MEMCG is already on in GKI. # These two BREAK the kABI and no patch covers them: they resize scheduler and # cgroup structures, which changes the CRC of thousands of exported symbols. # Stock vendor modules then refuse to load and the device bootloops. # Leave them commented out unless you rebuild EVERY kernel module from the # same source and flash vendor_boot, vendor_dlkm and system_dlkm together # with the new boot.img, all at once. # CONFIG_CFS_BANDWIDTH=y # CONFIG_CGROUP_PIDS=y Step 3: Build, flash, check # Build with Bazel, the AOSP build scripts or plain make , whichever your tree uses, and flash the result. Your stock vendor modules keep working because the ABI did not move. Then open the Droidspaces app and run Settings , Requirements , Check Requirements . CPU and process limits on GKI # CONFIG_CFS_BANDWIDTH , which --cpus needs, and CONFIG_CGROUP_PIDS , which --pids-limit needs, change the size of scheduler and cgroup structures that almost every exported kernel function refers to. On a 5.15 GKI tree they changed the checksum of about four thousand exported symbols, and no padding trick covers that. Stock vendor modules then refuse to load and the device bootloops. Turn them on only if you can rebuild every kernel module on the device from the same source tree and configuration, and flash them in vendor_boot , vendor_dlkm and system_dlkm together with the new boot.img , all at once. If any module is a prebuilt with no source, you cannot. Do not disable CONFIG_MODVERSIONS or force-load modules to get past the check; the structures really did change. Without these two options everything else works. --cpus and --pids-limit are skipped with a warning and the app greys out the two toggles. Memory limits need only CONFIG_MEMCG , which GKI already has. Keeping a limited container out of swap also needs CONFIG_MEMCG_SWAP , plus swapaccount=1 on the kernel command line before 5.8 unless CONFIG_MEMCG_SWAP_ENABLED is set; without it the container can still spill into swap past its limit, the start log says so, and the app greys out Allow swap . What the check looks for # droidspaces check , and the app's Requirements screen, probe the running kernel rather than its config. What each probe needs, and what you lose without it: Probe Option Without it PID, mount, UTS and IPC namespaces CONFIG_NAMESPACES , CONFIG_PID_NS , CONFIG_UTS_NS , CONFIG_IPC_NS Containers cannot start. pivot_root, procfs, sysfs always present Containers cannot start. Seccomp CONFIG_SECCOMP , CONFIG_SECCOMP_FILTER Containers cannot start. devtmpfs CONFIG_DEVTMPFS Hardware access is unavailable. Cgroup namespace, cgroup v2 CONFIG_CGROUPS , cgroup v2 systemd containers misbehave. Loop device, ext4 CONFIG_BLK_DEV_LOOP , CONFIG_EXT4_FS Sparse image containers cannot mount. PTY, devpts, epoll, signalfd always present on Android Interactive sessions fail. Network namespace, veth, bridge CONFIG_NET_NS , CONFIG_VETH , CONFIG_BRIDGE Only host mode works. Without the bridge alone, NAT uses a direct veth. IPv6 NAT CONFIG_IP6_NF_NAT , CONFIG_IP6_NF_TARGET_MASQUERADE NAT containers are IPv4 only. Macvlan CONFIG_MACVLAN Macvlan mode is unavailable. OverlayFS CONFIG_OVERLAY_FS Volatile mode is unavailable. FUSE, TUN CONFIG_FUSE_FS , CONFIG_TUN FUSE filesystems and VPNs inside the container do not work. User namespaces CONFIG_USER_NS Allow Sandboxing is unavailable. Memory, CPU and process limits CONFIG_MEMCG , CONFIG_CFS_BANDWIDTH , CONFIG_CGROUP_PIDS , and no cgroup_disable= for them on the kernel command line That limit is skipped. Swap limit CONFIG_MEMCG_SWAP with swap accounting on, swapaccount=1 before 5.8 A memory-limited container can still use swap. CPU usage accounting CONFIG_CGROUP_CPUACCT on kernels before 4.15 info shows no CPU usage. Which kernel version to aim for # Version What to expect 3.10 to 3.18 The floor. Namespaces work, but systemd distributions might be unstable. Alpine, Artix or Gentoo with OpenRC is the safe choice. 4.4 to 4.19 Solid. Any distribution whose systemd is older than 258, and Docker inside containers. 5.4 to 5.10 Everything, including cgroup v2 and current distributions. 5.15 and newer Everything, with the best performance. Where to ask # Kernel questions get answered in the Telegram channel . The kernel's own option reference is the kernel documentation . Previous: Anland | Next: Recipes
